summary: A 1977 extension to FTP, called XSEN, that provides for sending a message to a logged-in user, with variants for mailing it normally. It adds new FTP commands with syntax like the existing MAIL command.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 737 proposes FTP commands for sending a message directly to a logged-in user. Other commands can mail the message if direct sending fails or combine sending with mailing.

subtitle: FTP commands for sending text to a logged-in user or mailing it as a fallback.

tldr.problem: Some systems could send messages directly to a logged-in user's terminal, and users wanted that capability to work across network sites.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 737 proposes XSEN to send to a terminal, XSEM to send and mail if sending fails, and XMAS to mail and send; all use the existing MAIL command syntax.
tldr.outcome: The note describes FTP message commands and reply behavior for systems that support them; it does not report broader adoption.

today: The unit records RFC 737's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It describes three FTP commands for terminal sending and mail behavior.

sections.title: Sending to a User's Terminal
sections.content:
Some systems had a SEND command or program that put a message directly on a user's terminal. SAIL and ITS had broadened this idea to reach users at other network sites, and their FTP servers added three commands with the same syntax as the existing MAIL command.

For MAIL, the sender gives a recipient name, then sends message text ending with a line containing only a period. The server returns a completion reply after the message text.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension takes a local feature that displays a message on a user's terminal and makes it available through FTP between network sites.

sections.title: XSEN, XSEM and XMAS
sections.content:
XSEN means “Send to terminal.” It returns failure reply 453 if the addressee is not logged in or is refusing messages. XSEM means “Send, Mail if can't”; it returns notification reply 009 if direct sending cannot be done and an attempt is made to mail instead.

XMAS means “Mail And Send” and has no special replies. For XSEM and XMAS, mailing determines success, not direct sending.
sections.plainLanguage: XSEN only tries the terminal. XSEM falls back to mail if the user cannot be reached, while XMAS combines mailing and sending.

sections.title: Short Messages Only
sections.content:
The RFC says there are no corresponding variants for MLFL. The author explains that messages sent this way are generally short and that the implementors did not want to add the extra work.

The extension therefore describes command behavior for message text through MAIL-style input, rather than adding the same send options for file-based mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension does not add MLFL versions of these commands. The authors considered this kind of terminal message generally short enough to use MAIL.
